# Beeswarm plots {#sec-beeswa} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_tetris()` Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_tetris()`, modeled on Tetris: a black well, the tetromino block colors as marks, and the pixel font Press Start 2P (bundled with the package) for the title. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false} ::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; color: #02577A;"} :::
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description A beeswarm plot shows each number as its own point, so we can see where the numbers fall in each group.[^beeswarm] The points for each group stay close together and fall to the left and right of the group's place on the `x` axis. The form the points make in each group is called a swarm.[^mirror] We can make a beeswarm plot with the [`ggbeeswarm`](https://github.com/eclarke/ggbeeswarm) code.[^ggbeeswarm] ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # pak::pak("eclarke/ggbeeswarm") library(ggbeeswarm) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: The Game Boy is a small computer for playing games that you hold in your hands. Tetris is a game where small pieces fall from the top, and you fit them together to make a full line from side to side and clear it. Tetris came with every Game Boy,[^bundled] and by the 90s everyone had a best game to talk about. We'll make up[^simulate] the number of lines cleared in 80 games by each of three players. `rnbinom()` picks how many lines each game clears from [a rule for numbers that can fall far from their average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution),[^nbinom] with a different average (`mu`) for each player: 25 lines for a casual player, 60 for a regular, and 120 for an expert. Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 240 games every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1989) # same 240 games every time the code runs tetris_games <- tibble( game_id = 1:240, # 240 different games of Tetris, one row each player = rep(c("Casual", "Regular", "Expert"), each = 80) # 80 games for each player type ) |> mutate( player = factor(player, levels = c("Casual", "Regular", "Expert")), # least to most skilled lines_cleared = rnbinom(n(), size = 5, # small size spreads the counts out mu = c(Casual = 25, Regular = 60, # average lines cleared Expert = 120)[as.character(player)] # (looked up for each player type) ) ) glimpse(tetris_games) #> Rows: 240 #> Columns: 3 #> $ game_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9,… #> $ player Casual, Casual, Casual, Ca… #> $ lines_cleared 42, 6, 21, 30, 15, 36, 31,… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A beeswarm plot shows every game as its own point, so we can see how far the numbers in each group fall from each other.[^spread] A count is how many times something happens. Lines cleared are counts, but they fall much farther from their average than the counts we saw before: one bad drop can end a game early, and one good run can keep it going for a long time. Below we'll move from the games, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula] ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first ten games (all from the casual player). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(tetris_games$lines_cleared, 10) #> [1] 42 6 21 30 15 36 31 9 26 30 ``` ::: ::: The casual player clears about 25 lines on average, but these games run from 6 to 42. The variance is a number for how far the numbers fall from the mean.[^variance] The numbers below show the variance for each player.[^summary] For counts that come at a set rate (like the number of books kids read, which we saw before),[^poisson] the variance would be close to the mean. Here the variance is many times larger than the mean, and the difference grows as the player gets better. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} tetris_games |> group_by(player) |> summarise(mean = mean(lines_cleared), variance = var(lines_cleared), min = min(lines_cleared), max = max(lines_cleared)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The beeswarms below compare our regular player's 80 games to 80 games picked from the set rate rule with the same average (60 lines).[^poisson-draw] The Poisson swarm stays close together around 60. The Negative binomial swarm runs from under 10 to more than two times the average, with a long line of great games at the top.[^tail] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} regular_games <- tibble( model = rep(c("Negative binomial", "Poisson"), each = 80), lines_cleared = c( tetris_games$lines_cleared[tetris_games$player == "Regular"], rpois(80, lambda = 60))) ggplot(regular_games, aes(x = model, y = lines_cleared)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(size = 1.6, color = "#00F0F0") + geom_hline(yintercept = 60, linetype = "dashed", color = "#F5F5F5") + annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 60, label = "Average: 60 lines", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, color = "#F5F5F5") + labs(title = "Same average, wider spread", x = NULL, y = "Lines cleared") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/draw_beeswarm-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: The [rule we used](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution)[^nbinom-name] is often used for counts that fall farther from their average than the set rate rule allows.[^overdispersion] It has two numbers in it,[^params] an average ($\mu$) and a size ($r$), and its variance is: $$ X \sim \text{NB}(\mu, \; r = 5), \quad \text{Var}(X) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{r} $$ The first part ($\mu$) is the variance of the set rate rule, and the second part ($\mu^2 / r$) adds more on top.[^terms] For the regular player that's $60 + 3600 / 5 = 780$, but only 60 for the set rate rule. This extra part grows with $\mu^2$, so the expert's games ($\mu = 120$) fall much farther from their average than the casual player's ($\mu = 25$). As $r$ gets larger, the extra part gets smaller and our rule turns into the set rate rule.[^limit] Try `size = 500` in `rnbinom()` and the three swarms come in close. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()` - Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data` - Put `player` on the `x` axis - Put `lines_cleared` on the `y` axis - Add `ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm()` on top[^layer] (with `alpha`, so we can see through the points) ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_beeswarm <- labs( title = "Tetris", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Lines cleared in 80 games by each player", x = "Player", y = "Lines cleared") ggp2_beeswarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = 2 / 3, color = "#00F0F0") ggp2_beeswarm + labs_beeswarm ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: Below we change the form of the swarm with `method`. The `ggbeeswarm` code also has `geom_quasirandom()`, another way to place the points.[^shape] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ## More info Below are a few more things we can set[^args] and ways to make beeswarm plots. ### `method`
Use `method` to change the form of the beeswarm (`swarm`, `compactswarm`, `hex`, `square`, `center`, or `centre`) :::: {.column-margin} ::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"} Set the point `shape` to `21` so you can choose both its `fill` and its `color` ::: :::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_compact_swarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm( aes(fill = player), method = 'compactswarm', shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2/3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_compact_swarm + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_method-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `side`
To put the points on one side of each group only, use `side`.[^side] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_rside_swarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm( aes(fill = player), side = 1, # right side only shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2/3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_rside_swarm + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_side-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `cex`
The `cex` setting[^cex] controls the "*scaling for adjusting point spacing*" ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_beeswarm_cex <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm( aes(fill = player), cex = 1.6, shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2/3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_beeswarm_cex + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_cex-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `geom_jitter()`
`geom_jitter()` does not make a beeswarm. It moves each point to the side by a small amount picked by chance, so points can still land on top of each other. We set `width` to move the points to the side, and `height = 0` so no count moves up or down.[^jitter] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_jitter_swarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared)) + geom_jitter( aes(fill = player), height = 0, width = 0.11, shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2 / 3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_jitter_swarm + # add labels labs_beeswarm + labs(caption = "Simulated data; points jittered to the side at random") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_jitter-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: [^beeswarm]: The beeswarm plot displays the distribution of a continuous variable across the levels of a categorical variable. [^mirror]: The points are grouped by level and spread sideways along the categorical (`player`) axis, on both sides of each group by default, so the swarm takes the shape of the distribution (similar to a violin plot). [^ggbeeswarm]: The `ggbeeswarm` package. [^packages]: Install and load the packages. [^bundled]: Tetris came bundled with the Game Boy. [^simulate]: Simulate. [^nbinom]: A negative binomial distribution. [^seed]: Setting the random seed. [^spread]: The spread of each group, shown directly. [^formula]: The formula. [^variance]: The variance: the average squared distance from the mean (`var()`). [^summary]: Summary statistics: the mean, variance, minimum, and maximum for each player. [^poisson]: Poisson counts, like the Goosebumps books in @sec-overlapping-dot-plots. [^poisson-draw]: A Poisson distribution with $\lambda = 60$ (`rpois(80, lambda = 60)`). [^tail]: The negative binomial swarm stretches from single digits to more than twice the average, with a long right tail. [^nbinom-name]: The negative binomial distribution. [^overdispersion]: Overdispersion: counts more spread out than a Poisson distribution allows. [^params]: Its parameters: the mean $\mu$ and the size (or dispersion) parameter $r$. [^terms]: The first term is the Poisson variance; the second term is the extra variance. [^limit]: As $r \to \infty$, the negative binomial converges to the Poisson. [^labels]: Labels. [^layer]: Add the `geom_beeswarm()` layer. [^shape]: `geom_quasirandom()` spreads the points with a quasirandom sequence instead of placing them one by one; we don't show it here. [^args]: Additional arguments. [^side]: The `side` argument: `0` (the default) uses both sides, `1` the right side only, and `-1` the left side only. [^cex]: The `cex` argument. [^jitter]: `geom_jitter()` adds random noise to each point's position (`width` sideways, `height` up and down). It is a contrast to a beeswarm, not a beeswarm, and the jitter is noted in the caption.
